title: You've been putting it off
hook: Marcus: remember how long you've delayed, and that your time has a limit (Meditations 2.4)
tomorrow: as if it were the last

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard ending: the goldsmith's fate, read as allegory, and an honest flinch. Your line was hard to read. What did you hold both ways? Day one hundred seventy-four.

Everybody has a list. The call to the old friend. The doctor's appointment. The drawer, the will, the apology, the book you swore you'd start. It's been on the list so long it's practically furniture. You don't even see it anymore. And each time you pass it, a small voice says, soon. Almost two thousand years ago, the emperor of Rome had the same list, and the same voice. And in his notebook he turned around and argued with it. Today, you've been putting it off.
screen: `THE LIST THAT'S BECOME FURNITURE.` → `A SMALL VOICE SAYS SOON.` → `YOU'VE BEEN PUTTING IT OFF.`

segments.voice: Book two, section four, begins in George Long's translation: "Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it." Notice who he's talking to. Not his generals, not his son. Himself. The emperor, with an army at his command, is scolding himself for procrastinating. What things? Not paperwork. For Marcus, these things were the work of the philosopher: clearing his mind, living by reason, being just and calm and kind. He kept meaning to get serious about it. Then the passage turns. He tells himself: understand what kind of universe you're a part of, and remember that a limit of time is fixed for you. If you don't use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will go, and you will go, and it will not come back. That's the Stoic move. They didn't think about death to be gloomy. They thought about it to wake up. The limit isn't a threat; it's a clock you can finally hear. Every tradition in this path has its own version of this. The Psalms ask God to teach us to number our days. The Buddha's last words, in the old accounts, urge his followers to strive on with diligence. Marcus puts it in a single, blunt thought: you have been given chance after chance, and the chances are not endless. And here's the gentle part. He doesn't say you're a failure for putting it off. He just says, remember. The list is still there. Today still counts. There is a limit, and you're inside it now.
screen: `HOW LONG HAVE YOU PUT IT OFF?` · `AN EMPEROR SCOLDS HIMSELF.` · `A LIMIT OF TIME IS FIXED.` · `NOT GLOOM: A CLOCK YOU CAN HEAR.` · then, large: `THERE IS A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one delayed thing. Settle, and breathe. Let your list come to mind, and choose one item that's been waiting far too long. Something small enough to begin today. Picture yourself actually doing the first step: the text typed, the number dialed, the drawer open. Feel how light it would be to have it done. Then decide exactly when you'll do it, and say the time inside. The bell holds the time.
You've been putting it off. Marcus in Meditations 2.4, reminding himself how many chances he's had, and that his time has a limit. Today's word.
screen: `YOU'VE BEEN PUTTING IT OFF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: there is a limit. Today, do the one delayed thing you chose, at the time you chose, and cross it off where you can see it. Day one hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 174 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AS IF IT WERE THE LAST.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often return to 2.4 as a morning reminder, and many in modern Stoic practice keep a short daily reflection on the limits of time, sometimes called memento mori.

myth: Marcus wrote 2.4 to scold his generals
he wrote it to himself. the emperor is scolding his own procrastination.
the Stoics thought about death to wake up, not to be gloomy
the limit is a clock you can finally hear.

fork.setup: you're emperor, and you notice you've been putting off the work of living well for years. what do you do?
options: decide to start after the war.
write yourself a reminder that your time has a limit.
fork.reveal: Marcus writes it down: remember how long you've delayed, and that a limit of time is fixed. not a threat, a wake-up.

trapdoor: what you thought: a productivity tip from ancient Rome.
what it means: a reminder that your chances to live well are many, but not endless.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 2.4: the universe you belong to, and a fixed term of time; Stoic meditation on death as a spur to philosophy.
